content:
PROLOGUE

"FATHER, … this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent."

"God our Saviour desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth."

"There is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" - than the name of JESUS.

I. The life of man - to know and love God

God, infinitely perfect and blessed in himself, in a plan of sheer goodness freely created man to make him share in his own blessed life. For this reason, at every time and in every place, God draws close to man. He calls man to seek him, to know him, to love him with all his strength. He calls together all men, scattered and divided by sin, into the unity of his family, the Church. To accomplish this, when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son as Redeemer and Saviour. In his Son and through him, he invites men to become, in the Holy Spirit, his adopted children and thus heirs of his blessed life.

So that this call should resound throughout the world, Christ sent forth the apostles he had chosen, commissioning them to proclaim the gospel: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you; and lo, I am with you always, to the close of the age." Strengthened by this mission, the apostles "went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message by the signs that attended it."

Those who with God's help have welcomed Christ's call and freely responded to it are urged on by love of Christ to proclaim the Good News everywhere in the world. This treasure, received from the apostles, has been faithfully guarded by their successors. All Christ's faithful are called to hand it on from generation to generation, by professing the faith, by living it in fraternal sharing, and by celebrating it in liturgy and prayer.

facets.text: The Catechism opens by defining the ultimate purpose of human existence: God, infinitely perfect and blessed in himself, freely created man out of sheer goodness to share in his own blessed life. Man's vocation is therefore to know, love, and seek God with all his strength. This gratuitous divine initiative, not any human necessity, is the foundation of the whole economy of salvation.
facets.question: Why did God create man according to the Catechism's Prologue?

facets.text: The Prologue frames eternal life as knowledge of God and of Jesus Christ, citing John 17:3, 'this is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.' It joins this to 1 Timothy 2:4, that God 'desires all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,' and Acts 4:12, that there is 'no other name under heaven' by which we must be saved than Jesus. These three texts anchor the Catechism's teaching in the universality of God's salvific will centered on Christ.
facets.question: Which Scripture passages ground the Catechism's opening teaching on eternal life and salvation?

facets.text: God's saving plan unfolds in stages: he calls scattered and divided humanity into the unity of his family, the Church, and in the fullness of time sends his Son as Redeemer and Saviour. Through the Son and in the Holy Spirit, God invites men to become his adopted children and heirs of his blessed life. This presents salvation as trinitarian adoption and gathering into ecclesial communion.
facets.question: How does the Catechism describe God's plan to unite humanity through his Son and the Holy Spirit?

facets.text: The Prologue grounds the Church's mission in the Great Commission of Matthew 28:19-20, where Christ sends the apostles to make disciples of all nations, baptizing in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and teaching them to observe all he commanded, with the promise 'I am with you always, to the close of the age.' It adds Mark 16:20, that the apostles preached everywhere while the Lord confirmed the message by accompanying signs. This establishes the apostolic and missionary origin of catechesis itself.
facets.question: What is the scriptural basis for the Church's missionary and teaching mandate in the Prologue?

facets.text: The deposit of faith is described as a treasure received from the apostles and faithfully guarded by their successors, indicating apostolic succession and the continuity of Tradition. All the faithful are called to hand it on from generation to generation. This transmission occurs by professing the faith, living it in fraternal sharing, and celebrating it in liturgy and prayer.
facets.question: How is the faith transmitted from the apostles across generations according to the Prologue?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The Prologue to the Catechism sets out the purpose of human life as knowing and loving God, the trinitarian and Christocentric plan of salvation, and the apostolic mission to transmit the faith. Its scope is foundational, orienting the entire Catechism toward God's gratuitous call and the Church's task of handing on the deposit of faith.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: God, perfect and blessed in himself, freely created man out of sheer goodness to share his blessed life; man's vocation is to know and love him.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The opening triad of John 17:3, 1 Timothy 2:4, and Acts 4:12 anchors eternal life, universal salvific will, and salvation in the name of Jesus.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Salvation is presented as trinitarian adoption—the Father gathering scattered humanity into the Church, sending the Son as Redeemer, making men heirs in the Holy Spirit.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The Great Commission (Mt 28:19-20) and Mk 16:20 ground the Church's missionary, baptismal, and teaching mandate as the origin of catechesis.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The deposit of faith, received from the apostles and guarded by their successors, is transmitted by all the faithful through profession, fraternal living, liturgy, and prayer.
